title: The 25 most promising robotics startups in 2026, according to investors
excerpt: We asked investors from Sequoia, Felicis, Bessemer, and more to highlight promising robotics startups, as the sector sees an investment boom in 2026.
content_html:
By Rya Jetha

After years of investors shunning hardware, Silicon Valley is getting physical.

Robotics has become one of the hottest bets in tech as investors look beyond software for the next wave of AI. Physical AI startups — companies building machines that can act in the real world — raised a record $16.3 billion across 492 deals in the first quarter of 2026, according to PitchBook data.

Falling hardware costs, labor shortages, and pressure to reshore manufacturing are fueling a new generation of companies building for the physical world.

For Business Insider’s inaugural list of the most promising robotics startups, we asked 14 investors across the robotics venture ecosystem — from early-stage specialists to partners at Bain Capital Ventures, Sequoia Capital, and Bessemer Venture Partners — to identify the most promising robotics startups of 2026.

Each investor was asked to make two picks: one company from their portfolio and one in which they have no financial interest.

Their choices show how broad the robotics boom has become. Some startups on the list build general-purpose AI "brains" for robots, including FieldAI, Generalist, and Skild. Others develop humanoids for factories and homes, like Unitree, Walden, and Sunday Robotics. Another group applies robotics to specific jobs like metalworking, drug development, and strawberry picking. The list stretches from companies fresh out of the Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator to one preparing to go public.

Robotics is still a nascent field, and some of the technology is unproven. Researchers previously told Business Insider that humanoids, for instance, are a "fantasy product" with little near-term viability and that general-purpose home robots are still many years away.

Here are the 25 robotics startups investors are watching in 2026. The list is alphabetical.

Avatar Robotics

Nominated by: Amy Yin, defy.vc (an investor)

Total funding: $6.5 million, according to the company

What it does: San Francisco-based Avatar Robotics uses remotely operated robots to sort and pack products in warehouses. The company uses data from those shifts to train its robots to become more autonomous.

Why it's promising: Avatar's robots generate training data while doing paid work for customers. Human operators in Mexico and the Philippines control them with virtual reality headsets and handheld controllers, and Avatar uses those sessions to improve its robotics models.

CEO Colin Webb previously told Business Insider that this approach produces more useful data than paying people to collect it separately. His long-term goal is to build an "unlimited workforce for industrial labor" and have millions of robots deployed across factories, farms, and mines.

Cobot

Nominated by: Ben Hemani, Bison Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $160 million, according to the company

What it does: Santa Clara, California-based Cobot builds Proxie, a mobile robot that works alongside people in hospitals, factories, and logistics centers to move carts and materials. Its latest version has two arms for carrying and restocking items.

Why it's promising: Cobot is led by Brad Porter, who previously ran Amazon Robotics and served as CTO of Scale AI. Its first-generation robots logged nearly 13,000 hours and moved more than 154,000 carts for customers, including Mayo Clinic and Maersk, Porter said.

Those deployments shaped a second-generation Proxie that is more compact, can lift more than 200 pounds, and is cheaper to build because it has fewer parts.

Hemani of Bison Ventures told Business Insider that Proxie's autonomy stands out. A worker can, for example, write a cart's destination on an attached whiteboard, and Proxie can read it and deliver the cart there autonomously.

Dash Bio

Nominated by: Mark Martin, Cybernetix Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $47.5 million, according to the company

What it does: Boston-based Dash Bio automates lab testing for drug development. Its robots and software handle work that scientists do manually, such as preparing samples and running tests, helping pharmaceutical companies deliver results faster.

Why it's promising: Dash Bio was cofounded by Dave Johnson, Moderna's former chief data and AI officer. Dash can complete testing in days, around 10 times as fast as industry norms, Johnson told Business Insider. The company has a few dozen customers and publishes fixed pricing online, avoiding a lengthy sales process.

Dexterity

Nominated by: Kahini Shah, Obvious Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $295 million, according to the company

What it does: Bay Area-based Dexterity is building a general-purpose AI "brain" designed to control many kinds of robots.

Why it's promising: Dexterity's flagship product, Mech, is an "industrial superhumanoid," CEO Samir Menon told Business Insider. It has large arms and an extended reach for tasks such as loading trucks and stacking boxes onto pallets. Mech can load roughly 400 boxes into a trailer, compared with an industry average of about 300. The robots are powered by Foresight, Dexterity's AI model, which decides in real time how best to arrange packages inside a truck.

FedEx recently expanded its deployment of Dexterity's robots at its Maryland hub after several years of testing. Menon said Dexterity's systems are deployed at around 10 sites, with a similar number of pilots underway.

FieldAI

Nominated by: Alexandra Sukin, Bessemer Venture Partners (not an investor)

Total funding: $405 million, according to the company

What it does: Founded in 2023, FieldAI is building a single AI system that can control different types of robots and help them operate safely and autonomously in unpredictable environments.

Why it's promising: FieldAI has more than 30 customers, including construction firms, data center operators, and defense companies. CEO Ali Agha told Business Insider in June that the company has secured more than $100 million in revenue and customer contracts.

The company's software evaluates risk and makes decisions in unfamiliar situations without extensive task-specific training. The company has recruited from Google DeepMind, Waymo, Tesla, Nvidia, Boston Dynamics, and Amazon.

Foxglove

Nominated by: Alexandra Sukin, Bessemer Venture Partners (an investor)

Total funding: $60 million, according to the company

What it does: San Francisco-based Foxglove builds software for robotics companies, helping teams analyze data from its robots, identify failures, and improve performance.

Why it's promising: CEO Adrian Macneil got the idea for Foxglove while leading infrastructure engineering at Cruise, where he said less than 1% of the data collected across millions of miles was useful for improving its self-driving system.

"I realized that every robotics company would eventually need the same foundational data infrastructure, and they shouldn't have to spend years building it themselves," Macneil told Business Insider.

Foxglove now has more than 250 customers, including autonomous driving startup Wayve and defense tech companies Anduril, Shield AI, and Saronic.

Generalist

Nominated by: Siddharth Ramakrishnan, Scale Venture Partners (an investor)

Total funding: $540 million, according to the company

What it does: Bay Area-based Generalist builds AI software that can control different robots across factories, laboratories, and homes.

Why it's promising: Former Google DeepMind and Boston Dynamics roboticists founded Generalist. To teach its AI about the physical world, the startup built low-cost "grippers" that mimic robot hands and distributed thousands of them around the world, collecting more than 500,000 hours of training data.

CEO Pete Florence told Business Insider that the approach is working. He said Generalist's first model, GEN-0, improved as the company added more data and computing power. Florence compared its latest model, GEN-1, to GPT-3 because some uses, including folding laundry and packing iPhones into boxes, are now becoming commercially viable.

Gecko Robotics

Nominated by: Mark Martin, Cybernetix Ventures (not an investor)

Total funding: $347 million, according to the company

What it does: Pittsburgh-based Gecko Robotics builds wall-climbing robots and AI software to inspect power plants, pipelines, and naval ships.

Why it's promising: CEO Jake Loosararian started Gecko after visiting a power plant in college and learning how dangerous manual inspections could be for humans.

"If you want to digitize the physical world, you have to go about the hard effort of collecting data that's never been digitized before, and at a cost that isn't prohibitive," Loosararian told Business Insider. "That's where robots come in."

The company has since expanded to software that helps customers plan repairs and maintenance. In March, Gecko won a five-year contract with the US Navy and General Services Administration worth up to $71 million, starting with inspections of 18 Pacific Fleet ships.

GrayMatter

Nominated by: Ryan Gembala, Pathbreaker Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $86 million, according to the company

What it does: Carson, California-based GrayMatter Robotics builds AI-powered robots for surface finishing, a process that includes sanding, grinding, blasting, and coating manufactured parts. Its robots work on products ranging from guitars to fighter jets.

Why it's promising: Traditional industrial robots are typically programmed for a specific part and struggle when its shape, material, or condition changes. GrayMatter's robots scan each part, adapt on their own, and learn from every deployment. The company says its systems have generated more than 7 petabytes of manufacturing data, which it uses to improve its AI.

GrayMatter's customers include the US Air Force, Boeing, and Lockheed Martin. This month, the company announced a seven-year, $900 million agreement with two other robotics companies to automate shipbuilding work for the US Navy.

Machina Labs

Nominated by: Ryan Gembala, Pathbreaker Ventures (not an investor)

Total funding: $169 million, according to the company

What it does: Los Angeles-based Machina Labs builds robotic factories to make complex metal parts. Its RoboCraftsman system uses two robotic arms, sensors, and AI to shape, inspect, trim, and drill parts directly from digital designs.

Why it's promising: Ed Mehr, who previously worked at SpaceX, leads Machina. The company builds what Mehr calls a "software-defined factory" that can switch between making different products without costly retooling.

"You can program that facility to make missile components in the morning, and then in the afternoon you make aircraft components, and then at night when nobody's there you make automotive components," Mehr told Business Insider last month.

Machina is building a 200,000-square-foot factory with room for 50 RoboCraftsman cells. Last month, the company won a contract with Lockheed Martin to qualify its manufacturing process for parts used in JASSM, a long-range cruise missile used by the US military.

Matter

Nominated by: Charly Mwangi, Eclipse (an investor and cofounder)

Total funding: Undisclosed

What it does: Bay Area-based Matter is building autonomous factories that assemble drones and robots.

Why it's promising: Matter was cofounded by a team with experience at Tesla, Rivian, and Travis Kalanick's Atoms, and is being incubated by Eclipse partner Charly Mwangi, who previously held executive roles at all three companies. The startup has opened a 54,000-square-foot factory in Sunnyvale, California, and begun producing robotic components for customers.

"The goal is to rebuild American manufacturing as a software problem, not a labor problem," CEO Adi Prasad told Business Insider last month.

Matter says each production run generates data that improves MatterOS, its platform for automating and coordinating factory operations.

Mecka AI

Nominated by: Charly Mwangi, Eclipse (not an investor)

Total funding: $68 million, according to the company

What it does: New York City-based Mecka AI collects training data for robotics companies by capturing how humans interact with the physical world. People record everyday tasks using phones and wearable devices, and Mecka turns the recordings into datasets for training robots.

Why it's promising: Mecka aims to make physical-world data as inexpensive and easy to collect as the text and images used to train traditional AI models.

Instead of relying on people to control robots, Mecka puts sensors on humans to capture the visual, movement, and force data that cameras miss. It works with leading AI labs and is building custom hardware, including gloves with built-in sensors, for data collection. Mecka recently crossed $100 million in annualized revenue, CEO Josh Gao told Business Insider.

Mimic

Nominated by: Ben Hemani, Bison Ventures (not an investor)

Total funding: $20 million, according to the company

What it does: Zurich-based Mimic Robotics builds dexterous robotic hands and AI for complex industrial tasks. Workers use wearable gloves to demonstrate tasks, and Mimic's software trains robots to replicate those movements.

Why it's promising: Mimic spun out of an ETH Zurich research lab two years ago. The startup is working with manufacturers, including Audi, which is testing its technology in factories. The company says that its five-fingered robotic hand, which can handle more than 55 pounds, is not far off human capabilities in speed, dexterity, and strength. The startup is one of several trying to solve what Elon Musk has called the "hands problem" — recreating the dexterity of the human hand with sensors, motors, and software.

Noble Machines

Nominated by: Ally Warson, UP.Partners (an investor)

Total funding: Undisclosed

What it does: Bay Area-based Noble Machines builds general-purpose humanoid robots for hazardous and physically demanding industrial work. Its Moby robot is designed for jobs in manufacturing, construction, and energy plants.

Why it's promising: Engineers from Apple, SpaceX, and NASA founded Noble Machines in 2024. In less than two years, the company has built three generations of its humanoid robot and is finishing a fourth.

CEO Wei Ding told Business Insider that Noble has a deal to deploy its humanoids with a major global construction company. The startup is also developing AI that could eventually let customers teach a robot a new skill as quickly as it takes to train a new employee.

To reduce geopolitical risk and compete globally, Noble maintains two supply chains for its humanoids: one in Asia and another across the US and allied countries.

Palatial

Nominated by: Lyna Kim, Lowercarbon Capital (invested personally)

Total funding: Undisclosed

What it does: San Francisco-based Palatial automates the creation of virtual environments where robots can practice tasks before attempting them in the real world.

Why it's promising: Steven Ren got the idea while working on a digital twin of Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory, a virtual model used to plan and coordinate construction. Building it was slow and manual, and Ren saw an opportunity to automate the process. He soon concluded that robotics was an even bigger market than construction — a building needs one digital twin, while training a robot requires millions of simulated objects and environments.

Since launching its automated simulation generator earlier this year, Ren told Business Insider that more than 200 AI companies have expressed interest, with many — including Nvidia — becoming customers.

Skild AI

Nominated by: Stephanie Zhan, Sequoia (an investor); James Detweiler, Felicis (an investor)

Total funding: $2.2 billion, according to PitchBook

What it does: Skild AI builds an AI model designed to control robotic arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and mobile robots. The model is designed to help different machines learn new jobs without being programmed for each task.

Why it's promising: Former Carnegie Mellon professors Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta founded Skild. The company generated $30 million in revenue in 2025. Its technology is used in security, construction, warehouses, and manufacturing. Skild is working with Nvidia and Foxconn to use its AI to control robotic arms on production lines for Nvidia's Blackwell chips, automating an assembly task that is currently performed by people.

Sunday Robotics

Nominated by: Amanda Huang, Bain Capital Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $200 million, according to the company

What it does: Bay Area-based Sunday Robotics builds Memo, a wheeled robot that performs household chores.

Why it's promising: Last month, Sunday said Memo, powered by its new AI model, folded laundry in unfamiliar homes with a success rate above 99%.

"I think 2026 will be when the timeline for autonomous home robots shrinks in a very drastic way because of this breakthrough," CEO and cofounder Tony Zhao, a former Stanford robotics researcher, told Business Insider last month.

Sunday plans to place Memo in homes through a beta program this fall. It is also training Memo to vacuum, organize toys, and make coffee.

Synphony

Nominated by: Lyna Kim, Lowercarbon Capital (an investor)

Total funding: $8 million, according to the company

What it does: Bay Area-based Synphony collects real-world data and builds software that adapts robotics foundation models to specific industrial jobs. Its first challenge: teaching robots to pick strawberries.

Why it's promising: Synphony participated in Y Combinator earlier this year and finished the program with more than $1 million in revenue, CEO and cofounder Sean Wu told Business Insider. For its first pilot, the startup put data-collection gloves on strawberry pickers at a farm run by one of the largest US producers, then used the data to train a robot to pick the fruit.

Synphony plans to expand into other industrial tasks, including meat processing and warehouse packing.

Unitree

Nominated by: Stephanie Zhan, Sequoia (not an investor)

Total funding: $265 million, according to PitchBook

What it does: Hangzhou, China-based Unitree builds humanoid and four-legged robots for research, consumer, and industrial uses.

Why it's promising: Founded in 2016 by CEO Wang Xingxing, Unitree has shown that humanoid robots can be built relatively cheaply and at scale. It shipped more than 5,500 humanoids in 2025, more than a quarter of the global market, according to the company. Unitree is preparing to go public in Shanghai at a valuation of about $9 billion, potentially making it China's first publicly listed humanoid robotics company. It plans to invest in developing new hardware and software and expanding manufacturing.

Upside Robotics

Nominated by: Siddharth Ramakrishnan, Scale Venture Partners (not an investor)

Total funding: $7.5 million, according to PitchBook

What it does: Waterloo, Canada-based Upside Robotics builds small, solar-powered robots that apply fertilizer directly to plants. They use sensors and software to determine how much fertilizer each plant needs rather than applying the same amount everywhere.

Why it's promising: The company says its robots can cut fertilizer use by up to 70% by delivering nutrients directly to plant roots. Built-in cameras and sensors also monitor crop health.

Walden Robotics

Nominated by: Jim Adler, Toyota Ventures (an investor)

Total funding: $300 million, according to the company

What it does: Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Walden Robotics, which spun out of the Toyota Research Institute, builds general-purpose robots and the AI models that control them.

Why it's promising: Walden deploys robots in factories and warehouses to perform repetitive, physically demanding tasks such as loading car parts, cleaning machinery, and preparing components for assembly. CEO Russ Tedrake told Business Insider that the robots move on wheels rather than legs for greater safety and stability, and to leave room for a larger battery and more computing power.

"It's a pragmatic version of a humanoid," said Tedrake, who is a longtime MIT roboticist whose former students hold leadership roles at Boston Dynamics, Google DeepMind, Generalist, and Sunday Robotics.

Adler said he's bullish on Walden because of Tedrake's experience and the company's early traction. Within months of launching in January, its robots were handling eight-hour shifts at customer sites, he said

Westmag

Nominated by: Jim Adler, Toyota Ventures (not an investor)

Total funding: $11 million, according to the company

What it does: South San Francisco-based Westmag, short for Western Magnetics Company, makes motors and actuators for drones and robots.

Why it's promising: China dominates production of many of these components, but Westmag, with a seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz, is developing a US-made alternative to reduce manufacturers' reliance on overseas suppliers. The company is now ramping up production at its first factory south of San Francisco.

"The Western drone and robot companies we serve need reliable, cost-effective, and resilient component supply in order to scale and win globally," Jordan Sanders, cofounder and COO of Westmag, told Business Insider.

XDOF

Nominated by: Amanda Huang, Bain Capital Ventures (not an investor); James Detweiler, Felicis (not an investor); Kahini Shah, Obvious Ventures (invested personally)

Total funding: $78.33 million, according to PitchBook

What it does: XDOF collects and organizes real-world data used for training robots. It gathers data from people who control robots and perform everyday tasks.

Why it's promising: XDOF is tackling one of robotics' biggest bottlenecks: getting enough high-quality, real-world training data. Cofounder and CEO Philipp Wu founded the company after encountering a shortage of training data while researching robot learning at the University of California, Berkeley. XDOF now works with about 20 customers, including leading AI labs. Its investors include Thrive Capital, Spark Capital, and Andreessen Horowitz.

Huang from Bain Capital Ventures said that XDOF stands out because it understands that the hardware used to collect training data — from cameras to rig design to tracking algorithms — directly affects data quality. "Garbage in, garbage out," she said.

Zipline

Nominated by: Ally Warson, UP.Partners (not an investor)

Total funding: $2 billion, according to PitchBook

What it does: Bay Area-based Zipline builds and operates autonomous delivery drones that carry medical supplies, food, and retail goods.

Why it's promising: Zipline, which launched in Rwanda in 2016 to deliver blood, is now expanding in the US. The company said that the number of businesses offering delivery through its service grew 13 times in the first half of this year. Now, Zipline has hired executives from Tesla, Waymo, and Uber to scale its business.

1Robot

Nominated by: Amy Yin, defy.vc (not an investor)

Total funding: $11.05 million, according to the company

What it does: Bay Area-based 1Robot builds software that coordinates people, robots, autonomous vehicles, and AI agents to complete real-world tasks. For example, its software could use camera footage to detect a collision, have an AI agent assess the scene, and dispatch an autonomous vehicle with the right robots and personnel.

Why it's promising: 1Robot's customers include Samsung, Nestlé, and government agencies, cofounder and co-CEO Jesse Tran told Business Insider. Revenue reached $5.5 million in the first half of 2026, up from $2.5 million in all of 2025, he said.

Yin from defy.vc said 1Robot also stands out for its Vietnam- and Taiwan-based supply chain, which gives US customers an alternative to Chinese robotics hardware.

"Our future wars are going to be fought with humanoid robotics," she said.

This month, the company announced a seven-year, $900 million agreement with two other robotics companies to automate shipbuilding work for the US Navy. Machina Labs Machina Labs' RoboCraftsman. Machina Labs Nominated by: Ryan Gembala, Pathbreaker Ventures (not an investor)Total funding: $169 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Los Angeles-based Machina Labs builds robotic factories to make complex metal parts. Its RoboCraftsman system uses two robotic arms, sensors, and AI to shape, inspect, trim, and drill parts directly from digital designs.Why it's promising: Ed Mehr, who previously worked at SpaceX, leads Machina. The company builds what Mehr calls a "software-defined factory" that can switch between making different products without costly retooling."You can program that facility to make missile components in the morning, and then in the afternoon you make aircraft components, and then at night when nobody's there you make automotive components," Mehr told Business Insider last month.Machina is building a 200,000-square-foot factory with room for 50 RoboCraftsman cells. Last month, the company won a contract with Lockheed Martin to qualify its manufacturing process for parts used in JASSM, a long-range cruise missile used by the US military. Matter Matter CEO Adi Prasad. Adi Prasad Nominated by: Charly Mwangi, Eclipse (an investor and cofounder)Total funding: UndisclosedWhat it does: Bay Area-based Matter is building autonomous factories that assemble drones and robots.Why it's promising: Matter was cofounded by a team with experience at Tesla, Rivian, and Travis Kalanick's Atoms, and is being incubated by Eclipse partner Charly Mwangi, who previously held executive roles at all three companies. The startup has opened a 54,000-square-foot factory in Sunnyvale, California, and begun producing robotic components for customers."The goal is to rebuild American manufacturing as a software problem, not a labor problem," CEO Adi Prasad told Business Insider last month.Matter says each production run generates data that improves MatterOS, its platform for automating and coordinating factory operations. Mecka AI Mecka AI cofounders Jason Chong, Mogen Cheng, Josh Gao, and Duy Nguyen. Mecka AI Nominated by: Charly Mwangi, Eclipse (not an investor)Total funding: $68 million, according to the companyWhat it does: New York City-based Mecka AI collects training data for robotics companies by capturing how humans interact with the physical world. People record everyday tasks using phones and wearable devices, and Mecka turns the recordings into datasets for training robots.Why it's promising: Mecka aims to make physical-world data as inexpensive and easy to collect as the text and images used to train traditional AI models.Instead of relying on people to control robots, Mecka puts sensors on humans to capture the visual, movement, and force data that cameras miss. It works with leading AI labs and is building custom hardware, including gloves with built-in sensors, for data collection. Mecka recently crossed $100 million in annualized revenue, CEO Josh Gao told Business Insider. Mimic Mimic cofounders Stephan-Daniel Gravert, Stefan Weirich, and Elvis Nava. Mimic Nominated by: Ben Hemani, Bison Ventures (not an investor)Total funding: $20 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Zurich-based Mimic Robotics builds dexterous robotic hands and AI for complex industrial tasks. Workers use wearable gloves to demonstrate tasks, and Mimic's software trains robots to replicate those movements.Why it's promising: Mimic spun out of an ETH Zurich research lab two years ago. The startup is working with manufacturers, including Audi, which is testing its technology in factories. The company says that its five-fingered robotic hand, which can handle more than 55 pounds, is not far off human capabilities in speed, dexterity, and strength. The startup is one of several trying to solve what Elon Musk has called the "hands problem" — recreating the dexterity of the human hand with sensors, motors, and software. Noble Machines Noble Machines' team. Noble Machines Nominated by: Ally Warson, UP.Partners (an investor)Total funding: UndisclosedWhat it does: Bay Area-based Noble Machines builds general-purpose humanoid robots for hazardous and physically demanding industrial work. Its Moby robot is designed for jobs in manufacturing, construction, and energy plants.Why it's promising: Engineers from Apple, SpaceX, and NASA founded Noble Machines in 2024. In less than two years, the company has built three generations of its humanoid robot and is finishing a fourth.CEO Wei Ding told Business Insider that Noble has a deal to deploy its humanoids with a major global construction company. The startup is also developing AI that could eventually let customers teach a robot a new skill as quickly as it takes to train a new employee.To reduce geopolitical risk and compete globally, Noble maintains two supply chains for its humanoids: one in Asia and another across the US and allied countries. Palatial Palatial cofounders Krish Mehta and Steven Ren. Palatial Nominated by: Lyna Kim, Lowercarbon Capital (invested personally)Total funding: UndisclosedWhat it does: San Francisco-based Palatial automates the creation of virtual environments where robots can practice tasks before attempting them in the real world.Why it's promising: Steven Ren got the idea while working on a digital twin of Tesla's Nevada Gigafactory, a virtual model used to plan and coordinate construction. Building it was slow and manual, and Ren saw an opportunity to automate the process. He soon concluded that robotics was an even bigger market than construction — a building needs one digital twin, while training a robot requires millions of simulated objects and environments.Since launching its automated simulation generator earlier this year, Ren told Business Insider that more than 200 AI companies have expressed interest, with many — including Nvidia — becoming customers. Skild AI Skild AI cofounders Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta. Skild AI Nominated by: Stephanie Zhan, Sequoia (an investor); James Detweiler, Felicis (an investor)Total funding: $2.2 billion, according to PitchBookWhat it does: Skild AI builds an AI model designed to control robotic arms, humanoids, quadrupeds, and mobile robots. The model is designed to help different machines learn new jobs without being programmed for each task.Why it's promising: Former Carnegie Mellon professors Deepak Pathak and Abhinav Gupta founded Skild. The company generated $30 million in revenue in 2025. Its technology is used in security, construction, warehouses, and manufacturing. Skild is working with Nvidia and Foxconn to use its AI to control robotic arms on production lines for Nvidia's Blackwell chips, automating an assembly task that is currently performed by people. Sunday Robotics Sundary Robotics' Memo robot. Sunday Robotics Nominated by: Amanda Huang, Bain Capital Ventures (an investor)Total funding: $200 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Bay Area-based Sunday Robotics builds Memo, a wheeled robot that performs household chores.Why it's promising: Last month, Sunday said Memo, powered by its new AI model, folded laundry in unfamiliar homes with a success rate above 99%."I think 2026 will be when the timeline for autonomous home robots shrinks in a very drastic way because of this breakthrough," CEO and cofounder Tony Zhao, a former Stanford robotics researcher, told Business Insider last month.Sunday plans to place Memo in homes through a beta program this fall. It is also training Memo to vacuum, organize toys, and make coffee. Synphony Synphony's team. Synphony Nominated by: Lyna Kim, Lowercarbon Capital (an investor)Total funding: $8 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Bay Area-based Synphony collects real-world data and builds software that adapts robotics foundation models to specific industrial jobs. Its first challenge: teaching robots to pick strawberries.Why it's promising: Synphony participated in Y Combinator earlier this year and finished the program with more than $1 million in revenue, CEO and cofounder Sean Wu told Business Insider. For its first pilot, the startup put data-collection gloves on strawberry pickers at a farm run by one of the largest US producers, then used the data to train a robot to pick the fruit.Synphony plans to expand into other industrial tasks, including meat processing and warehouse packing. Unitree Unitree's humanoid robot. Shi Ying/VCG via Getty Images Nominated by: Stephanie Zhan, Sequoia (not an investor)Total funding: $265 million, according to PitchBookWhat it does: Hangzhou, China-based Unitree builds humanoid and four-legged robots for research, consumer, and industrial uses.Why it's promising: Founded in 2016 by CEO Wang Xingxing, Unitree has shown that humanoid robots can be built relatively cheaply and at scale. It shipped more than 5,500 humanoids in 2025, more than a quarter of the global market, according to the company. Unitree is preparing to go public in Shanghai at a valuation of about $9 billion, potentially making it China's first publicly listed humanoid robotics company. It plans to invest in developing new hardware and software and expanding manufacturing. Upside Robotics Nominated by: Siddharth Ramakrishnan, Scale Venture Partners (not an investor)Total funding: $7.5 million, according to PitchBookWhat it does: Waterloo, Canada-based Upside Robotics builds small, solar-powered robots that apply fertilizer directly to plants. They use sensors and software to determine how much fertilizer each plant needs rather than applying the same amount everywhere.Why it's promising: The company says its robots can cut fertilizer use by up to 70% by delivering nutrients directly to plant roots. Built-in cameras and sensors also monitor crop health. Walden Robotics Walden's robot. Pat Piasecki for Walden Nominated by: Jim Adler, Toyota Ventures (an investor)Total funding: $300 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Cambridge, Massachusetts-based Walden Robotics, which spun out of the Toyota Research Institute, builds general-purpose robots and the AI models that control them.Why it's promising: Walden deploys robots in factories and warehouses to perform repetitive, physically demanding tasks such as loading car parts, cleaning machinery, and preparing components for assembly. CEO Russ Tedrake told Business Insider that the robots move on wheels rather than legs for greater safety and stability, and to leave room for a larger battery and more computing power."It's a pragmatic version of a humanoid," said Tedrake, who is a longtime MIT roboticist whose former students hold leadership roles at Boston Dynamics, Google DeepMind, Generalist, and Sunday Robotics.Adler said he's bullish on Walden because of Tedrake's experience and the company's early traction. Within months of launching in January, its robots were handling eight-hour shifts at customer sites, he said Westmag Westmag cofounders Jordan Sanders and David Hansen. Westmag Nominated by: Jim Adler, Toyota Ventures (not an investor)Total funding: $11 million, according to the companyWhat it does: South San Francisco-based Westmag, short for Western Magnetics Company, makes motors and actuators for drones and robots.Why it's promising: China dominates production of many of these components, but Westmag, with a seed round led by Andreessen Horowitz, is developing a US-made alternative to reduce manufacturers' reliance on overseas suppliers. The company is now ramping up production at its first factory south of San Francisco."The Western drone and robot companies we serve need reliable, cost-effective, and resilient component supply in order to scale and win globally," Jordan Sanders, cofounder and COO of Westmag, told Business Insider. XDOF Nominated by: Amanda Huang, Bain Capital Ventures (not an investor); James Detweiler, Felicis (not an investor); Kahini Shah, Obvious Ventures (invested personally)Total funding: $78.33 million, according to PitchBookWhat it does: XDOF collects and organizes real-world data used for training robots. It gathers data from people who control robots and perform everyday tasks.Why it's promising: XDOF is tackling one of robotics' biggest bottlenecks: getting enough high-quality, real-world training data. Cofounder and CEO Philipp Wu founded the company after encountering a shortage of training data while researching robot learning at the University of California, Berkeley. XDOF now works with about 20 customers, including leading AI labs. Its investors include Thrive Capital, Spark Capital, and Andreessen Horowitz.Huang from Bain Capital Ventures said that XDOF stands out because it understands that the hardware used to collect training data — from cameras to rig design to tracking algorithms — directly affects data quality. "Garbage in, garbage out," she said. Zipline Zipline drone. Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Nominated by: Ally Warson, UP.Partners (not an investor)Total funding: $2 billion, according to PitchBookWhat it does: Bay Area-based Zipline builds and operates autonomous delivery drones that carry medical supplies, food, and retail goods.Why it's promising: Zipline, which launched in Rwanda in 2016 to deliver blood, is now expanding in the US. The company said that the number of businesses offering delivery through its service grew 13 times in the first half of this year. Now, Zipline has hired executives from Tesla, Waymo, and Uber to scale its business. 1Robot 1Robot cofounders Jesse Tran and Son Le. 1Robot Nominated by: Amy Yin, defy.vc (not an investor)Total funding: $11.05 million, according to the companyWhat it does: Bay Area-based 1Robot builds software that coordinates people, robots, autonomous vehicles, and AI agents to complete real-world tasks. For example, its software could use camera footage to detect a collision, have an AI agent assess the scene, and dispatch an autonomous vehicle with the right robots and personnel.Why it's promising: 1Robot's customers include Samsung, Nestlé, and government agencies, cofounder and co-CEO Jesse Tran told Business Insider. Revenue reached $5.5 million in the first half of 2026, up from $2.5 million in all of 2025, he said.Yin from defy.vc said 1Robot also stands out for its Vietnam- and Taiwan-based supply chain, which gives US customers an alternative to Chinese robotics hardware."Our future wars are going to be fought with humanoid robotics," she said. 在投资者多年来回避硬件之后，硅谷正在变得实体化。

随着投资者将目光投向软件之外的下一波人工智能浪潮，机器人技术已成为科技领域最热门的赌注之一。 根据 PitchBook 的数据，物理人工智能初创公司——制造可以在现实世界中行动的机器的公司——在 2026 年第一季度通过 492 笔交易筹集了创纪录的 163 亿美元。

硬件成本下降、劳动力短缺以及制造业回流的压力正在推动新一代公司为现实世界建设。

在 Business Insider 首次发布的最有前途的机器人初创公司名单中，我们询问了机器人风险投资生态系统中的 14 名投资者——从早期专家到贝恩资本风险投资公司 (Bain Capital Ventures)、红杉资本 (Sequoia Capital) 和 Bessemer Venture Partners 的合作伙伴 - 以确定 2026 年最有前途的机器人初创公司。

每个投资者都被要求做出两项选择：一项是他们投资组合中的公司，另一项是他们没有经济利益的公司。

他们的选择表明机器人技术的繁荣已经变得多么广泛。 名单上的一些初创公司为机器人构建通用人工智能“大脑”，包括 FieldAI、Generalist 和 Skild。 其他公司则为工厂和家庭开发类人机器人，例如 Unitree、Walden 和 Sunday Robotics。 另一个小组将机器人技术应用于金属加工、药物开发和草莓采摘等特定工作。 这份名单涵盖了刚从硅谷创业加速器 Y Combinator 出来的公司以及准备上市的公司。

机器人技术仍然是一个新兴领域，一些技术尚未得到证实。 研究人员此前曾告诉《商业内幕》，例如，类人机器人是一种“幻想产品”，短期内几乎没有可行性，而通用家用机器人还需要很多年的时间。

以下是投资者在 2026 年关注的 25 家机器人初创公司。 该列表按字母顺序排列。

阿凡达机器人

提名人：Amy Yin，defy.vc（投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：650万美元

公司业务：总部位于旧金山的 Avatar Robotics 使用远程操作的机器人对仓库中的产品进行分类和包装。 该公司利用这些班次的数据来训练其机器人，使其变得更加自主。

为什么它有前途：阿凡达的机器人在为客户做有偿工作的同时生成训练数据。 墨西哥和菲律宾的操作员通过虚拟现实耳机和手持控制器来控制它们，阿凡达利用这些会话来改进其机器人模型。

首席执行官科林·韦伯此前告诉《商业内幕》，这种方法产生的数据比花钱让人单独收集数据更有用。 他的长期目标是建立“无限的工业劳动力队伍”，并在工厂、农场和矿山部署数百万台机器人。

Cobot

提名人：Ben Hemani，Bison Ventures（投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：1.6亿美元

公司业务：总部位于加利福尼亚州圣克拉拉的 Cobot 开发了 Proxie，这是一款移动机器人，可以与医院、工厂和物流中心的人员一起移动手推车和材料。 它的最新版本有两个手臂，用于携带和补充物品。

为什么它有前途：Cobot 由 Brad Porter 领导，他之前负责 Amazon Robotics 并担任 Scale AI 的首席技术官。 波特说，其第一代机器人已工作近 13,000 小时，并为梅奥诊所和马士基等客户搬运了超过 154,000 辆推车。

这些部署塑造了第二代 Proxie，它更加紧凑，可以举起超过 200 磅的重量，而且由于零件较少，制造成本也较低。

Bison Ventures 的 Hemani 告诉 Business Insider，Proxie 的自主权非常突出。 例如，工作人员可以在附加的白板上写下购物车的目的地，Proxie 可以读取它并自动将购物车运送到那里。

达世生物

提名人：Mark Martin，Cyber​​netix Ventures（投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：4750万美元

业务：总部位于波士顿的 Dash Bio 实现药物开发实验室测试的自动化。 它的机器人和软件处理科学家手动完成的工作，例如准备样品和运行测试，帮助制药公司更快地提供结果。

为什么它有前途：Dash Bio 由 Moderna 前首席数据和人工智能官戴夫·约翰逊 (Dave Johnson) 共同创立。 约翰逊告诉《商业内幕》，达世币可以在几天内完成测试，大约是行业标准速度的 10 倍。 该公司拥有几十个客户，并在网上发布固定定价，避免了漫长的销售过程。

灵巧

提名人：Kahini Shah，Obvious Ventures（投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：2.95 亿美元

业务：位于湾区的 Dexterity 正在构建一个通用人工智能“大脑”，旨在控制多种机器人。

为什么它有前途：首席执行官萨米尔·梅农 (Samir Menon) 告诉《商业内幕》，Dexterity 的旗舰产品 Mech 是一个“工业超人”。 它具有大臂和延伸范围，可以执行诸如装载卡车和将箱子堆放在托盘上等任务。 Mech 可以将大约 400 个箱子装入拖车，而行业平均水平约为 300 个。 这些机器人由 Dexterity 的人工智能模型 Foresight 提供支持，该模型实时决定如何最好地在卡车内安排包裹。

经过几年的测试，联邦快递最近在马里兰州枢纽扩大了 Dexterity 机器人的部署。 Menon 表示，Dexterity 的系统部署在大约 10 个地点，并且正在进行类似数量的试点。

现场人工智能

提名人：Alexandra Sukin，Bessemer Venture Partners（非投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：4.05 亿美元

业务：FieldAI 成立于 2023 年，正在构建一个单一的人工智能系统，可以控制不同类型的机器人，并帮助它们在不可预测的环境中安全、自主地操作。

为什么有前途：FieldAI 拥有 30 多家客户，包括建筑公司、数据中心运营商和国防公司。 首席执行官 Ali Agha 6 月份告诉 Business Insider，该公司已获得超过 1 亿美元的收入和客户合同。

该公司的软件可以评估风险并在不熟悉的情况下做出决策，而无需进行大量的特定任务培训。 该公司已从谷歌 DeepMind、Waymo、特斯拉、英伟达、波士顿动力和亚马逊招募了人才。

毛地黄

提名人：Alexandra Sukin，Bessemer Venture Partners（投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：6000万美元

公司业务：总部位于旧金山的 Foxglove 为机器人公司构建软件，帮助团队分析机器人的数据、识别故障并提高性能。

为什么它有前途：首席执行官阿德里安·麦克尼尔(Adrian Macneil)在领导 Cruise 的基础设施工程时产生了 Foxglove 的想法，他表示，在数百万英里内收集的数据中，只有不到 1% 对于改进其自动驾驶系统有用。

麦克尼尔告诉《商业内幕》：“我意识到，每个机器人公司最终都需要相同的基础数据基础设施，他们不应该花费数年时间自己构建它。”

Foxglove 目前拥有超过 250 家客户，包括自动驾驶初创公司 Wayve 以及国防科技公司 Anduril、Shield AI 和 Saronic。

通才

提名人：Siddharth Ramakrishnan，Scale Venture Partners（投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：5.4亿美元

公司业务：总部位于湾区的 Generalist 开发人工智能软件，可以控制工厂、实验室和家庭中的不同机器人。

为什么它有前途：前谷歌 DeepMind 和波士顿动力机器人专家创立了 Generalist。 为了让人工智能了解物理世界，这家初创公司制造了模仿机器人手的低成本“抓手”，并将数千个抓手分发到世界各地，收集了超过 500,000 小时的训练数据。

首席执行官皮特·弗洛伦斯 (Pete Florence) 告诉《商业内幕》，这种方法正在发挥作用。 他表示，随着公司增加更多数据和计算能力，Generalist 的第一个模型 GEN-0 得到了改进。 Florence 将其最新型号 GEN-1 与 GPT-3 进行了比较，因为一些用途（包括折叠衣物和将 iPhone 装入盒子中）现已变得商业可行。

壁虎机器人

提名人：Mark Martin，Cyber​​netix Ventures（非投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：3.47 亿美元

公司业务：总部位于匹兹堡的 Gecko Robotics 制造爬墙机器人和人工智能软件来检查发电厂、管道和海军舰艇。

为什么它有前途：首席执行官 Jake Loosararian 在大学参观了一家发电厂并了解到手动检查对人类有多么危险后创立了 Gecko。

“如果你想将物理世界数字化，你就必须付出艰苦的努力来收集以前从未数字化过的数据，而且成本也不算太高，”卢萨里安告诉《商业内幕》。 “这就是机器人发挥作用的地方。”

此后，该公司已扩展到帮助客户计划维修和维护的软件。 今年 3 月，Gecko 赢得了美国海军和总务管理局一份价值高达 7100 万美元的五年合同，首先对 18 艘太平洋舰队舰艇进行检查。

灰质

提名人：Ryan Gembala，Pathbreaker Ventures（投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：8600万美元

业务：总部位于加利福尼亚州卡森的 GrayMatter Robotics 制造人工智能驱动的机器人进行表面精加工，该过程包括打磨、研磨、喷砂和涂层制造零件。 它的机器人负责处理从吉他到战斗机等各种产品。

为什么它有前途：传统的工业机器人通常是针对特定零件进行编程的，当其形状、材料或条件发生变化时，机器人就会陷入困境。 GrayMatter 的机器人扫描每个部件，自行适应，并从每次部署中学习。 该公司表示，其系统已生成超过 7PB 的制造数据，用于改进人工智能。

GrayMatter 的客户包括美国空军、波音公司和洛克希德·马丁公司。 本月，该公司宣布与另外两家机器人公司达成一项为期七年、价值 9 亿美元的协议，为美国海军实现造船工作的自动化。

机械实验室

提名人：Ryan Gembala，Pathbreaker Ventures（非投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：1.69 亿美元

业务：位于洛杉矶的 Machina Labs 建造机器人工厂来制造复杂的金属零件。 其 RoboCraftsman 系统使用两个机械臂、传感器和人工智能，直接根据数字设计对零件进行成型、检查、修剪和钻孔。

为什么它很有前途：Ed Mehr 曾在 SpaceX 工作过，现在领导 Machina。 该公司建立了梅尔所说的“软件定义工厂”，可以在制造不同产品之间进行切换，而无需进行昂贵的重组。

梅尔上个月对《商业内幕》表示：“你可以对该设施进行编程，使其在早上制造导弹部件，然后在下午制造飞机部件，然后在晚上没人的时候制造汽车部件。”

Machina 正在建设一座占地 200,000 平方英尺的工厂，可容纳 50 个 RoboCraftsman 单元。 上个月，该公司赢得了洛克希德·马丁公司的一份合同，以验证其用于美国军方使用的远程巡航导弹 JASSM 的零部件制造工艺。

事情

提名人：Charly Mwangi，Eclipse（投资者兼联合创始人）

资金总额：未公开

业务：总部位于湾区的 Matter 正在建设组装无人机和机器人的自主工厂。

为什么它有前途：Matter 是由一支在特斯拉、Rivian 和 Travis Kalanick 的 Atoms 拥有丰富经验的团队共同创立的，并由 Eclipse 合作伙伴 Charly Mwangi 孵化，Charly Mwangi 此前曾在这三家公司担任高管职务。 该初创公司在加利福尼亚州桑尼维尔开设了一家占地 54,000 平方英尺的工厂，并开始为客户生产机器人组件。

首席执行官阿迪·普拉萨德（Adi Prasad）上个月对《商业内幕》表示：“我们的目标是将美国制造业重建为软件问题，而不是劳动力问题。”

Matter 表示，每次生产运行都会生成可改进 MatterOS 的数据，MatterOS 是其用于自动化和协调工厂运营的平台。

麦加人工智能

提名人：Charly Mwangi，Eclipse（非投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：6800万美元

业务：总部位于纽约的 Mecka AI 通过捕捉人类与物理世界的互动方式，为机器人公司收集训练数据。 人们使用手机和可穿戴设备记录日常任务，Mecka 将记录转化为训练机器人的数据集。

为什么它有前途：Mecka 的目标是让物理世界的数据像用于训练传统人工智能模型的文本和图像一样便宜且易于收集。

Mecka 没有依靠人来控制机器人，而是在人身上安装传感器来捕捉相机遗漏的视觉、运动和力数据。 它与领先的人工智能实验室合作，正在构建定制硬件，包括用于数据收集的内置传感器的手套。 Mecka 首席执行官乔什·高 (Josh Takah) 告诉《商业内幕》，最近年收入突破了 1 亿美元。

Mimic

提名人：Ben Hemani，Bison Ventures（非投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：2000万美元

公司业务：总部位于苏黎世的 Mimic Robotics 为复杂的工业任务打造灵巧的机械手和人工智能。 工人们使用可穿戴手套来演示任务，Mimic 的软件训练机器人复制这些动作。

为什么它有前途：两年前，Mimic 从苏黎世联邦理工学院的一个研究实验室中分离出来。 该初创公司正在与包括奥迪在内的制造商合作，奥迪正在工厂测试其技术。 该公司表示，其五指机器人手可以承受超过 55 磅的重量，在速度、灵活性和力量方面与人类能力相差不远。 该初创公司是几家试图解决埃隆·马斯克所说的“手问题”的初创公司之一，即通过传感器、电机和软件重现人手的灵巧性。

高贵机器

提名人：Ally Warson，UP.Partners（投资者）

资金总额：未公开

业务：总部位于湾区的 Noble Machines 制造通用人形机器人，用于危险和体力要求较高的工业工作。 其 Moby 机器人专为制造、建筑和能源工厂的工作而设计。

为什么它充满希望：来自 Apple、SpaceX 和 NASA 的工程师于 2024 年创立了 Noble Machines。 在不到两年的时间里，该公司已经制造出了三代人形机器人，并且正在完成第四代。

首席执行官丁伟告诉《商业内幕》，Noble 已与一家大型全球建筑公司达成协议，部署其人形机器人。 该初创公司还在开发人工智能，最终可以让客户像培训新员工一样快速地教授机器人新技能。

为了降低地缘政治风险并在全球范围内竞争，Noble 为其人形机器人维持着两条供应链：一条位于亚洲，另一条横跨美国及其盟国。

富丽堂皇的

提名人：Lyna Kim，Lowercarbon Capital（个人投资）

资金总额：未公开

业务：总部位于旧金山的 Palatial 自动创建虚拟环境，机器人可以在虚拟环境中练习任务，然后再在现实世界中尝试执行任务。

为什么它有前途：Steven Ren 在开发特斯拉内华达超级工厂的数字孪生时产生了这个想法，这是一个用于规划和协调建设的虚拟模型。 构建它是缓慢且手动的，Ren 看到了自动化该过程的机会。 他很快得出结论，机器人技术是比建筑更大的市场——一栋建筑需要一个数字孪生，而训练机器人需要数百万个模拟物体和环境。

任正非告诉 Business Insider，自今年早些时候推出自动模拟生成器以来，已有 200 多家人工智能公司表达了兴趣，其中包括 Nvidia 在内的许多公司都成为了客户。

技能人工智能

提名人：Stephanie Zhan，红杉资本（投资人）； James Detweiler, Felicis（投资者）

根据 PitchBook 的数据，融资总额：22 亿美元

用途：Skild AI 构建了一个人工智能模型，旨在控制机械臂、人形机器人、四足动物和移动机器人。 该模型旨在帮助不同的机器学习新的工作，而无需针对每项任务进行编程。

为什么它有前途：前卡内基梅隆大学教授 Deepak Pathak 和 Abhinav Gupta 创立了 Skild。 该公司 2025 年收入为 3000 万美元。 其技术用于安全、建筑、仓库和制造。 Skild 正在与 Nvidia 和富士康合作，利用其人工智能来控制 Nvidia Blackwell 芯片生产线上的机械臂，从而实现目前由人工执行的组装任务的自动化。

周日机器人

提名人：Amanda Huang，Bain Capital Ventures（投资者）

据该公司称，融资总额：2亿美元

公司业务：总部位于湾区的 Sunday Robotics 制造了 Memo，这是一款执行家务的轮式机器人。

为什么它有前途：上个月，Sunday 表示，Memo 在其新的人工智能模型的支持下，在陌生的家里折叠衣物，成功率超过 99%。

首席执行官兼联合创始人、前斯坦福大学机器人研究员托尼·赵上个月对《商业内幕》表示：“我认为，由于这一突破，到 2026 年，自主家庭机器人的开发时间将大幅缩短。”

Sunday 计划今年秋天通过测试计划将 Memo 放置在家庭中。 它还训练 Memo 吸尘、整理玩具和煮咖啡。

交响乐

提名人：Lyna Kim，Lowercarbon Capital（投资者）

据该公司称，总资金：800万美元

业务：总部位于湾区的 Synphony 收集现实世界的数据并构建软件，使机器人基础模型适应特定的工业工作。 它的第一个挑战：教机器人采摘草莓。

为什么它充满希望：Synphony 首席执行官兼联合创始人 Sean Wu 告诉《商业内幕》，今年早些时候，Synphony 参与了 Y Combinator，并以超过 100 万美元的收入完成了该计划。 在其第一个试点中，这家初创公司为美国最大生产商之一经营的农场的草莓采摘者戴上数据收集手套，然后使用这些数据训练机器人采摘水果。

Synphony 计划扩展到其他工业任务，包括肉类加工和仓库包装。

尤尼树

提名人：Stephanie Zhan，红杉资本（非投资者）

根据 PitchBook 的数据，总资金：2.65 亿美元

上行机器人

根据 PitchBook 的数据，总资金：750 万美元

公司业务：总部位于加拿大滑铁卢的 Upside Robotics 制造小型太阳能机器人，可以直接向植物施肥。 他们使用传感器和软件来确定每株植物需要多少肥料，而不是在所有地方都施用相同的肥料量。

为什么它有前途：该公司表示，其机器人可以将养分直接输送到植物根部，从而减少高达 70% 的化肥用量。 内置摄像头和传感器还可以监测作物健康状况。

瓦尔登机器人公司

为什么它有前途：瓦尔登在工厂和仓库中部署机器人来执行重复性的、体力要求较高的任务，例如装载汽车零件、清洁机械以及准备组装组件。 首席执行官 Russ Tedrake 告诉《商业内幕》，机器人通过轮子而不是腿移动，以提高安全性和稳定性，并为更大的电池和更强的计算能力留出空间。

XDOF

提名人：Amanda Huang，Bain Capital Ventures（非投资者）； James Detweiler，Felicis（非投资者）； Kahini Shah，Obvious Ventures（个人投资）

根据 PitchBook 的数据，总资金：7833 万美元

用途：XDOF 收集并组织用于训练机器人的真实数据。 它从控制机器人和执行日常任务的人那里收集数据。

为什么它有前途：XDOF 正在解决机器人技术的最大瓶颈之一：获得足够的高质量、真实世界的训练数据。 联合创始人兼首席执行官 Philipp Wu 在加州大学伯克利分校研究机器人学习时遇到训练数据短缺的情况后创立了该公司。 XDOF 目前与大约 20 个客户合作，其中包括领先的人工智能实验室。 其投资者包括 Thrive Capital、Spark Capital 和 Andreessen Horowitz。

贝恩资本风险投资公司的黄表示，XDOF 之所以脱颖而出，是因为它了解用于收集训练数据的硬件（从相机到装备设计到跟踪算法）直接影响数据质量。 “垃圾进来，垃圾出去，”她说。
